about.en:
The Arab Reading Challenge was launched by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum to build a reading habit in Arabic among school students. Over one school year each participant reads books outside the curriculum and writes a one-page summary of each in a series of coloured 'passports' (red, green, blue, silver and gold, ten books each), reaching 50 books by the end. The 10th cycle (2025-26) drew more than 40 million students from about 60 countries, and national champions were crowned in Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the other Arab states before the Dubai final in October 2026.

It is open to students from grade 1 to grade 12 in public and private schools. Students register through their school and a supervising teacher, who submits the passports. Schools then run internal selection, followed by district and national qualifiers organised with each ministry of education, where shortlisted readers are interviewed by judges on their books, comprehension and expression. National winners travel to Dubai for the final. Arab students living outside the Arab world, and students of determination, compete in their own categories.

Prizes include AED 500,000 for the overall champion, AED 1,000,000 shared in the Distinguished School award, AED 300,000 for distinguished supervisors and AED 100,000 for the community (diaspora) champion. Beyond the prizes, it is an easy, free way to build reading, writing and public-speaking skills in Arabic, and a national title is a strong line on any university application in the region.

en: Free and open to grades 1–12 in every Arab country, plus Arab students abroad
Read and summarise up to 50 books across five 'passports' during the school year
AED 500,000 champion prize and a final in Dubai

eligibility.en: School students from grade 1 to grade 12 who read in Arabic, in public or private schools in any participating country (including Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman). Arab students living in non-Arab countries can enter the community (jaliyat) track. Participation is through a registered school and supervisor.

en: Ask your school's Arabic department or librarian whether it is registered for the 2026-27 cycle
Register through your school and supervising teacher (schools sign up on the official website)
Collect your reading passports and summarise each book you read on one visa page
Complete as many passports as you can (50 books for all five) and hand them to your supervisor
Prepare for the school, district and national qualifying interviews in spring 2027

costs.en: Free. No entry fee; schools receive the passports. Travel to the Dubai final for national winners is arranged by the organisers.

score_reason: Free, huge, open to every school student in the Gulf with a big prize; national registration dates vary.

about.en:
The JA Company Program is INJAZ Bahrain's flagship entrepreneurship programme. With the guidance of volunteer consultants from local companies, high-school and university students start, organise and operate an actual enterprise: they elect a management team, raise share capital, design and produce a product or service, market and sell it, keep accounts and finally liquidate the company and report to shareholders. Sessions run weekly during the school year and are supported by online learning material.

INJAZ Bahrain was founded in 2005 as part of JA Worldwide (INJAZ Al-Arab in the Arab region) and works with the Ministry of Education and universities across the Kingdom. The 2026 cycle ended with the 18th Young Entrepreneurs Competition, in which more than 1,100 students took part; winning school and university companies go on to represent Bahrain at the INJAZ Al-Arab regional competition.

The programme builds teamwork, leadership, negotiation, accounting and public-presentation skills, and it gives students a real business record and contacts with mentors from banks and companies. It is a strong extracurricular for anyone thinking about business, economics or engineering.

en: Run a real student company for a full school year
Mentored by volunteers from Bahraini companies
Winners go to the national Young Entrepreneurs Competition and the INJAZ Al-Arab regional final

Or submit the student inquiry form on the INJAZ Bahrain website
Form a team and join the weekly sessions with your volunteer consultant
Launch, run and report on your company
Compete in the Young Entrepreneurs Competition in spring

costs.en: Free for students; programmes are funded by INJAZ Bahrain's corporate partners.

score_reason: Free, well-established, runs every year; mostly through partner schools.

about.en:
Reboot01 is an on-campus coding institute in Seef, Bahrain, built on the 01 Edu model (the same peer-to-peer, gamified method as 01 schools worldwide). There are no lectures: students learn by completing projects and 'quests' in teams, with the curriculum updated to current technologies. Graduates leave as full-stack developers, and the institute says they typically join companies at mid to senior level.

Admission has three stages. First you create an account and take a 90-minute online game test (memory and logic puzzles) that you can retake. Shortlisted candidates are invited to a full-time, four-week 'Selection Pool' in which they learn real coding material, sit weekly practical tests and do team assignments. Those who pass join the two-year professional programme; selection pools open several times a year, so there is no fixed semester.

No degree or coding background is required, only motivation and the ability to commit to two years. Training is supported by Tamkeen for Bahraini students, and payment plans are available for others. There is also a shorter AI Generalist workshop. It is a serious alternative or complement to a university computer-science degree for school leavers in the Gulf.

Project-based peer learning on the 01 Edu model
Rolling admission through an online game test

eligibility.en: Anyone aged 18 or over who has completed high school. No coding experience needed. Tamkeen funding applies to Bahraini nationals; non-Bahrainis can join with a payment plan. The programme is on campus in Bahrain.

Take the 90-minute online game test on a laptop (memory and logic games; retakes allowed)
If shortlisted, attend the four-week full-time Selection Pool
Pass the weekly practical tests and team assignments
Join the next two-year cohort

about.en:
Kilma ('word') is LOYAC's long-running youth debate programme. Over three weeks of evening sessions (Sunday to Thursday, 5–8 pm Kuwait time), participants learn active listening, critical thinking, building and rebutting arguments, structured debate, research, body language and confident public speaking. Each session takes a different theme, such as persuasion, leadership or teamwork, through discussions of local and global issues and interactive activities.

The November 2026 edition runs from 1 to 19 November at LOYAC (Aisha School, Qibla) and the National Bank of Kuwait. The language of instruction is Arabic. At the end, participants form teams and compete in a friendly debate tournament to apply what they have learned. Past participants rate it 4.9/5 on LOYAC's portal.

LOYAC is a Kuwaiti non-profit founded in 2002 that runs leadership, volunteering and professional programmes for young people, with chapters in Jordan, Lebanon and Yemen. Kilma is a good first step for students who want to join school debate or MUN teams.

en: Three weeks of evening debate and public-speaking training in Arabic
Ends with a friendly team debate competition
Run by LOYAC, Kuwait's best-known youth development non-profit

Open the Kilma programme page and register
Pay the programme fee to confirm your seat
Attend all sessions from 1 to 19 November

about.en:
Kontinue is LOYAC's social entrepreneurship programme for ambitious founders and early-stage startups. Over six intensive in-person weeks (Sunday to Wednesday, 5–9 pm, at Boursa Kuwait), participants learn to identify real user needs, write a value proposition, test the market, choose the right metrics and turn their idea into a workable business model, using established startup frameworks. Experts from different sectors run workshops on revenue, funding, legal basics and the founder mindset.

Each participant is paired one-to-one with a local entrepreneur as mentor for the whole programme, and teams are encouraged to build social impact into their ventures. The programme ends with a pitch of a viable MVP to a judging panel. Cash prizes are KWD 700 for first place, KWD 500 for second and KWD 300 for third. It is sponsored by Boursa Kuwait, Zain and Al Dau International Holding, and is taught in Arabic and English.

By the end, participants have a market-validated business idea that addresses a social challenge in Kuwait, an investor deck and a practised elevator pitch. It suits university students and young graduates who want structured support before applying to accelerators.

One-to-one mentor from Kuwait's founder community
Final MVP pitch with KWD 700 / 500 / 300 prizes

about.en:
Darb Al-Akhdar ('the green path') is LOYAC's paid green-skills internship, sponsored by AGFUND and hosted by the Palms Agro Production Company (PAPCO), a listed Kuwaiti agriculture and landscaping firm. From 1 to 16 November participants work 9 am–3 pm at PAPCO's farm in Amghara (a bus is provided), learning about Kuwait's agricultural sector, plant varieties that grow locally, open-field and greenhouse cultivation, and plant care. From 17 to 19 November they move to LOYAC for an introduction to permaculture and design a sustainable space.

The programme also builds time management, leadership, teamwork and communication skills. A minimum of 80 of the 84 hours is required to receive the stipend and certificate, absences are limited to one day, and travel during the programme is not allowed. Applicants must not be employed, should be interested in sustainability, and must complete or register for LOYAC's Green Volunteering programme to receive the reward.

It is a rare paid, hands-on entry point into agriculture and sustainability work in the Gulf, and useful for students considering environmental science, agriculture or architecture.

Hands-on farm and greenhouse work with PAPCO
Introduction to permaculture and sustainable design

about.en:
FLEX Global builds on the Future Leaders Exchange (FLEX) and the Kennedy-Lugar Youth Exchange and Study (YES) programmes and opens them to a wider set of countries. Funded by the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs and implemented by American Councils with AFS-USA, Amideast and iEARN, it places secondary-school students with volunteer host families across the United States for one academic year. Participants attend a local high school, take part in community service and 'American Excellence' activities on entrepreneurship, technology, government and leadership, and act as cultural ambassadors for their country.

Bahrain is on the 2027-28 country list. Recruitment began in autumn 2026, results are announced in spring 2027, finalists travel to the U.S. in summer 2027 and return in May or June 2028. Selection is merit-based over several rounds, including English testing, essays and interviews; the programme looks mainly for students who can adapt and thrive in a new environment, not for native-level English. Placement is mostly in suburban and rural communities and cannot be chosen.

There is no fee: the programme covers travel, the host-family placement, school, insurance and a monthly allowance. Because the old YES programme for the Gulf has been paused, FLEX Global is currently the main fully funded U.S. high-school year open to Bahraini students.

about.en:
The Arabic Language Scheme (ALS) is run by the British Omani Society with support from Oman's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Each year it sends ten British students and graduates to the Sultan Qaboos College for Teaching Arabic to Non-Native Speakers in Manah, about 20 minutes from the historic city of Nizwa. The 2027 scheme runs from 6 June to 29 July 2027.

Participants receive five hours of Arabic tuition a day, mainly in Modern Standard Arabic, plus classes and language-exchange sessions in the Omani dialect. They live full-board in the college's student hostel in a fully Arabic-speaking environment, and the programme includes excursions to Oman's mountains, deserts and coast and to sites such as Nizwa. It is aimed at recent graduates and young professionals with at least mid-intermediate Arabic who want to reach a higher level and build links with Oman.

The scheme is fully funded: return UK–Oman flights, accommodation and meals, visa and insurance, and a weekly allowance for day-to-day costs. Successful applicants join the Society (GBP 25 a year) and become part of the BOS alumni network, which is a useful route into Gulf-focused careers in diplomacy, business and research.

about.en:
OTF Scale is the ideation-stage vehicle of the Oman Future Fund. It writes the first cheque, up to OMR 40,000, released against a first experiment agreed with the founder. No deck, traction or company is required at application: the fund looks for a clearly defined problem, a founding team with a reason to solve it and a first experiment it can fund. It is sector-agnostic, with a portfolio of more than 40 startups in fintech, mobility, tourism, edtech, climate tech, deep tech/AI and more.

The process is fast: a 15-minute application on the Oman Future Fund investee platform, a working session (not a pitch) with OTF Scale and its partner Al Jabr in week one, diligence and a 90-day experiment plan in weeks two to four, and an investment committee decision in weeks five to six. In return the fund takes a minority stake on standard early-stage terms, without board control.

Beyond capital, founders get help with incorporation, legal, finance, hiring and pricing during their first 180 days, introductions across Omani government and industry, and access to accelerator programmes run with Al Jabr, with a path to follow-on capital from the wider Oman Future Fund network. It is one of the few funds in the Gulf that will back a student or graduate founder at the idea stage.

Selected startups first take 'Raise: The Art of Fundraising', a two-week evening bootcamp (four-hour classes) delivered by Spring Venture Services, which is backed by Bahrain's Al-Waha Fund of Funds and Hambro Perks. Modules cover the global investment ecosystem, funding rounds, equity crowdfunding, pitching to investors, key investment documents, data rooms, valuation, product-market fit and exit strategies, with hands-on workshops, fireside chats and one-to-one office hours.

The programme ends with a pitch night: each shortlisted startup pitches for several minutes and answers judges' questions in front of an audience, and the winner receives a cash prize released against milestones, with possible further support from partners. Past judges have included investors from Spring, MEVP, Shorooq and AWS.

It suits student and graduate founders who already have a minimum viable product and a registered company in Bahrain. StartUp Bahrain also runs the three-day StartUp Bahrain Weekend for people who are still at the idea stage (the 2026 edition was held in May with the University of Bahrain).

Today the catalogue is organised into career readiness, technology, personal development, business and entrepreneurship, and languages, with multi-course 'specialisations' and a separate K-12 education platform for school students. Courses are self-paced and can be followed on the web or the Edraak mobile app.

For students in Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the rest of the region it is an easy, free way to build skills in Arabic, prepare for university or the job market, and earn course certificates to show on CVs and applications. Check each course page for whether a certificate is free or paid.

The World Scholar's Cup (WSC) is a not-for-profit international academic programme for students aged about 10 to 18. Each season has one interdisciplinary theme (the 2026 theme is 'Are We There Yet?') with study guides across history, social studies, science and technology, art and music, literature and a special area. At each round, teams of three compete in four events: Team Debate, Collaborative Writing, the Scholar's Challenge (a multiple-choice test) and the Scholar's Bowl, a team quiz in a theatre with clickers.

The Kuwait Round takes place on 6–7 November 2026 at Al Nibras International Bilingual School. There are two divisions: juniors (up to 13) and seniors (14 and over, up to the final year of secondary school). Students can register as a school team, form mixed teams with students from other schools, or register individually and be matched with teammates. Most teams prepare for two to eight weeks. Teams that reach the qualifying threshold earn places at the Global Rounds (held June to August) and then at the Tournament of Champions at Yale University in November.

WSC is designed to reach well beyond a school's top three students, and it is a fun way to build debating, writing and research skills in English, meet students from across Kuwait and the region, and earn international medals. All study materials are free; each round charges a modest tournament fee that usually includes meals.

Committees include UNESCO, ECOFIN, UNEP, UNHCR, the Security Council and UN Women, two Arabic-language councils (the Arab Human Rights Committee and ALECSO), an International AI Governance Council, and creative councils such as FIA, FIFA, a Star Wars Galactic Senate, The Hunger Games and Marvel. It is a well-run, affordable entry point into MUN for students in Bahrain and nearby Gulf countries, with the unusual option of debating in Arabic as well as English.

Launched in September 2018, it offers about 5,000 video lessons in physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics and general science, covering curricula from kindergarten to grade 12, together with exercises and applications. The lessons were produced through the Translation Challenge, a large Arabic science-translation project in which hundreds of Arab volunteers translated, edited, voiced and adapted top international educational content to the curricula used in Arab countries.

In December 2020 a second phase added about 1,000 Arabic-language videos covering a full K-12 Arabic curriculum, plus cultural videos on Arabic literature and children's stories (also in the 'Madrasa Stories' app). Lessons are organised by grade and subject, with a searchable video library and 'missions' that let students earn points on a leaderboard.

The platform is free for more than 50 million Arab students wherever they are. For students in Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman it is a handy way to strengthen STEM foundations in Arabic before exams, olympiad selections or university.

Rwaq is an Arabic open-learning platform with more than 5.5 million active learners and over 21,000 learning components. Its catalogue spans economics, management and marketing; computer science and digital skills; literature and the Arabic language; creativity and innovation; and Islamic studies. Many courses are free and taught by university professors and practitioners, for example Business Fundamentals, Microsoft Excel, Computational Thinking, Generative AI for Everyone (Copilot and ChatGPT), Marketing Psychology, KPIs and OKRs, and Teaching Arabic to Non-Native Speakers.

Alongside free courses, Rwaq offers career-track programmes (data analyst, software engineer, UX designer, project manager, AI engineer, digital marketer, cybersecurity specialist) and preparation for professional certificates from Google, IBM, Microsoft, Meta and CompTIA, some of which are paid. It also runs a free Comprehensive Entrepreneurship Licence (ILFEN) track with live sessions, and a career-interest assessment.

For school leavers and university students in Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the wider Arab world, Rwaq is a flexible way to learn job-ready and academic skills in Arabic and add certificates to a CV.

about.en:
The National Bridge Building Competition, now in its third season, is organised by the Sabah Al-Ahmad Center for Giftedness and Creativity, a centre of the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences (KFAS). Teams apply physics and engineering principles to a real structure: using 200 wooden sticks, they must design and build a bridge model to exact specifications that spans a 40 cm gap and carries the maximum possible load.

The competition takes place on 4–5 December 2026 at the Joint Giftedness Academy (Boys). Day 1 (Friday) is a four-hour build session after a rules briefing. Day 2 (Saturday) includes team presentations and a design display, load testing in two groups and the awards ceremony. Bridges are judged on maximum load relative to the bridge's own weight and the amount of material used (Strength Award: KWD 400, 300 and 200), on innovation, elegance and function (Design Award: KWD 200), and on the team poster explaining the project (Best Poster: KWD 200). Teams may photograph their design process beforehand and complete their poster during the build.

It is a hands-on introduction to structural engineering that builds planning, design, creative thinking, teamwork, decision-making and time-management skills, and gives future engineering applicants a concrete national competition result.

STEM Racing (formerly F1 in Schools) is the world's largest STEM motorsport challenge, supported by Formula 1. In Kuwait it is run by the Sabah Al-Ahmad Center for Giftedness and Creativity (KFAS). For the 2026-27 season, SACGC's team visits schools to introduce students to designing, engineering and racing a scale Formula 1 car and helps them form teams.

The road has four stages: (1) the school books a visit; (2) teams register and progress through design and build checkpoints; (3) teams race their cars at the national competition; and (4) the top two teams represent Kuwait at the international competition in Singapore. Once at least 20 schools register (18 had registered at the time of checking), prizes unlock: a complete manufacturing room for the winning school and USD 5,000 in cash for the winning team, shared between mentor and students. SACGC also runs introductory STEM Racing workshops on aerodynamics using paper cars.

The challenge combines CAD design, aerodynamics, manufacturing, project management, branding and presentation, which makes it excellent preparation for engineering, design and business degrees.

about.en:
SACGC's Acceleration Program 2026 identifies Kuwaiti innovation addressing food and water security and moves high-potential projects towards validation, pilot readiness, commercialisation and international exposure. It is designed for projects beyond the idea stage, such as prototypes, MVPs, beta solutions or pilots; a registered company is not required. Target sectors include advanced food production, controlled environments, food safety and traceability, supply-chain resilience and alternative food systems, as well as smart irrigation, water reuse, leak detection and conservation technologies.

Stage 1 is the Kuwait Acceleration Sprint (16–23 November 2026): problem framing and validation, customer discovery and lean startup, food and water market insights, MVP development, business models, technical feasibility and pitch training, ending with a Pitch and Selection Day on 23 November. Stage 2 takes the top 10 finalists on an International Mission to Barcelona (8–17 December 2026) delivered with Mind the Bridge, a global open-innovation platform: one-to-one sessions with scaling managers, meetings with AgriTech, desalination and corporate innovation stakeholders, and an International Demo Day on 15 December.

It is open to university students with a capstone project in the field, activists, inventors and entrepreneurs, and is a rare chance for young Gulf innovators to get European ecosystem exposure.

about.en:
Through its Global Enrichment Program, the Sabah Al-Ahmad Center for Giftedness and Creativity (a KFAS centre) supports five Kuwaiti students to attend the Harvard Summer School Pre-College Program in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The programme offers two weeks of university-level academic exploration and discussion with students from around the world. Summer 2027 sessions run 21 June–2 July, 12–23 July and 26 July–6 August. Only STEM modules qualify for SACGC funding.

The process: apply directly to Harvard Summer School and obtain an unconditional acceptance; email the letter to SACGC for scholarship consideration and an interview; pay a non-refundable KWD 250 administrative fee to reserve the place; the parent pays Harvard and books the approved flight; then SACGC reimburses approved programme fees and round-trip economy airfare by bank transfer in the first week of the programme, after verifying enrolment. Families pay for health insurance and any visa.

The programme aims to help gifted students discover their capabilities, build research skills, gain cross-cultural experience and prepare for admission to leading universities.

Yale Young Global Scholars (YYGS) is a two-week residential academic programme at Yale University in New Haven for outstanding high-school students from around the world. Through its Global Enrichment Program, the Sabah Al-Ahmad Center for Giftedness and Creativity supports Kuwaiti students who are admitted to the Innovations in Science and Technology (IST) session, where they explore STEM topics, exchange ideas with peers from many countries and experience university-level learning. Summer 2027 sessions run 20 June–2 July, 4–16 July and 18–30 July.

The journey: attend a SACGC virtual information session (5 or 12 November 2026, 7–8 pm Kuwait time); apply to YYGS for the IST session by 6 January 2027; obtain an unconditional YYGS offer; submit it to SACGC for scholarship consideration and interview; confirm the place; then pay, book flights and attend. SACGC reimburses approved programme fees and economy airfare in the first week of the programme. A KWD 250 administrative fee applies, and families cover health insurance and visa. Students should wait for SACGC confirmation before paying anything.

YYGS is one of the most respected summer programmes for international students, and SACGC funding makes it accessible to high-achieving Kuwaiti students.

about.en:
The Kuwait Red Crescent Society (KRCS) treats volunteering as a fundamental pillar of its humanitarian mission. It recruits volunteers of all ages and especially seeks to increase youth participation, offering a motivating environment with structured programmes and specialised courses.

Volunteers are trained in first aid, disaster management and community services, and support KRCS relief programmes and campaigns in Kuwait and abroad. KRCS also runs public first-aid courses and a youth group, which can be contacted directly.

Volunteering with a national Red Crescent society builds practical emergency skills, teamwork and a record of sustained community service that is valued by universities and scholarship committees, particularly for students interested in medicine, public health or international affairs.

about.en:
The Technology Capacity Building (TCB) clubs are run by the Sabah Al-Ahmad Center for Giftedness and Creativity, a centre of the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement of Sciences. They offer short, hands-on technology courses at the Joint Giftedness Academy in Al-Sawaber (Kuwait City) and at science clubs in Al-Jahra and Al-Ahmadi, plus STEM Racing sessions at The Avenues mall.

The November 2026 schedule at Al-Sawaber alone lists about 25 courses, each running two or three weekday evenings (5–7 pm): Cubroid and Matata coding robots and electronic circuits for ages 6–10; cybersecurity basics and online ethics; an introduction to AI and machine learning; 3D design for 3D printing; Laser Makers; 'Design Your Website Using AI' and 3D modelling in Blender for ages 11–14; and Fischertechnik robotics and mechatronics for ages 9–13. Classes are small (around 8–13 seats) and taught mainly in Arabic.

At KWD 2 per course they are an easy, affordable way for younger students to try different areas of technology before committing to competitions such as WRO or STEM Racing.
